steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing a concept-based framework for ethical software design that goes beyond catalogs of dark patterns. Motivate the problem, explain the gap between research and practice and the limits of dark-pattern catalogs, introduce our concept-based approach, list the contributions, and give a roadmap of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Deceptive design and the term "dark pattern"
2. Research on dark patterns and the gap with practice
3. Catalogs vs. theories
4. Limitations of existing dark-pattern catalogs
5. Our approach: positive patterns based on software concepts
6. Contributions
7. Paper roadmap and evaluation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Deceptive design
- users feel annoyed/frustrated but also resigned; deception so rampant users have to live with it
- practitioners coined "dark pattern": label common deceptive tactics and idioms, catalog them, point to examples
- hope: exposure leads responsible designers to shun them

2. Research and the gap with practice
- incidence of dark patterns; user reactions; how designers choose to incorporate them (or not)
- theories of what makes a design "dark"
- gap between this research and designers' working practices
- causes: cultural divide (ethics discussions more academic); ethical guidelines hard to translate into practice, esp. subtle judgments on borderline cases
- less recognized: practitioners make fewer fresh design decisions than academics assume; mostly adoption (and adaptation) of large pieces of functionality and interaction design
- so pattern-driven "don't do things like this" may be more practical than theory-driven general criteria

3. Catalogs vs. theories: complementary
- catalogs readily actionable: easy to evaluate, matched to circumstances, applied straightforwardly
- theories: less immediately applicable, but underlying principles, ethical justification for consensus, language for edge cases

4. Limitations of catalogs
- (1) say what not to do, designers want to know what to do; community misses chance to publicize and inculcate good practices
- (2) variant designs sharing only some features, or presented subtly differently, hard to evaluate; e.g. "suggested items" in shopping cart vs. Sneak into Basket
- (3) necessarily incomplete; avoiding a set of dark patterns not sufficient for acceptability; challenge for regulation
- well-intentioned company that avoided known dark patterns should have some confidence it won't be sued over elements never explicitly specified
- worse with broad regulation, e.g. recent EU white paper: all forms of emotional steering culpable

5. Our approach
- combine aspects of patterns and theory
- acceptable designs = instantiations of positive patterns; deviations = "dark"
- patterns based on software concepts (introduced to modularize application functionality)
- concept: unit of functionality, coherent and separable service, clear purpose
- online store: ShoppingCart, Order, Catalog; less domain-specific: UserAuthentication, Notification, Recommendation
- propose concept catalogs: standard versions of concepts and their variants

6. Contributions
- (1) framework for evaluating designs (regulators, designers, critics): dark when user's expected concept doesn't match application concept; prior approaches use deviation from expectations but don't say how expectations are obtained; concepts play this role
- (2) language for consensus standards: industry standards for best practices, e.g. PCI payment security, Web accessibility; concept catalogs give structure and language for conventional behaviors/interfaces of common units like shopping carts
- (3) design method: collaborative creation of catalogs + instantiation of concepts in a particular design; Alexander's programme in architecture; realized in software (code level) by community from the design patterns book

7. Roadmap and evaluation
- Section 2: taxonomies and theories of dark patterns, differences and synergies
- Section 3.1 software concepts; Sections 3.2, 3.3 darkness criteria; Section 4 concept catalogs
- three studies: Brignull's catalog, latest version (5.1); three shopping cart variants (5.2); sample concept vs. variants in popular web applications (5.3)
- Section 6.1 merits, 6.2 challenges, Section 7 next steps

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
When users run into deceptive design elements in applications, they can feel annoyed or frustrated, but they also feel resigned. There is a feeling that deception is so rampant that users just have to live with it. To counter this, practitioners came up with the term "dark pattern" to label the common tactics and idioms that are used to deceive users. They catalogued them and pointed to examples, hoping that exposing them would lead responsible designers to avoid them.

Researchers have recognized that this problem is important. They have investigated how often dark patterns occur, explored how users react to them and how designers decide to incorporate them or not, and more broadly they have developed theories that try to articulate what exactly makes a design "dark". But while doing this, a gap has opened between this rich body of research and the working practices of designers.

Partly this is because of a cultural divide, where ethical discussions are more common in academic settings, and partly it is because ethical guidelines are not easy to translate into practice, especially when they need subtle judgments about borderline cases.

Another reason, which is less recognized but maybe equally important, is that practitioners spend less time making fresh design decisions than academics often think. A lot of their effort is adopting (and adapting) large pieces of functionality and interaction design. In this respect the pattern-driven approach, which says "don't do things like this", may be more practical than theory-driven approaches that give more general criteria.

So pattern catalogs and theories have complementary benefits. Catalogs can be acted on readily: their contents are easy to evaluate, and usually they can be matched to the given circumstances and applied straightforwardly. Theories are less immediately applicable, but they give the underlying principles and the ethical justification for consensus viewpoints, and also a language for exploring edge cases when consensus is harder to reach.

But the existing catalogs of dark patterns have limitations. First, and most obviously, they tell a designer what not to do, when a designer usually wants advice on what to do. This makes a catalog less useful, and it also means that the larger community of designers misses an opportunity to publicize and inculcate good practices.

Second, the match between a pattern and an exact instantiation may be clear, but it can be harder to evaluate variant designs that share only some of the features of the pattern, or that present them in subtly different ways. For example, it is not clear if adding "suggested items" to a user's shopping cart violates the Sneak into Basket dark pattern.

Third, a catalog of negative patterns is necessarily incomplete. Making sure that a particular set of dark patterns is absent from a design cannot be enough to establish that the design is acceptable. This is the challenge of regulating against dark patterns. A well-intentioned company that has avoided the known dark patterns in its products should surely be able to have some confidence that it will not be sued for including design elements that might come to be regarded as dark but were never explicitly specified. The broad nature of some regulatory efforts makes this problem worse (for example, a recent EU white paper suggests that all forms of emotional steering are culpable).

5. Our approach
- combine aspects of patterns and theory
- acceptable designs = instantiations of positive patterns; deviations = "dark"
- patterns based on software concepts (introduced to modularize application functionality)
- concept: unit of functionality, coherent and separable service, clear purpose
- online store: ShoppingCart, Order, Catalog; less domain-specific: UserAuthentication, Notification, Recommendation
- propose concept catalogs: standard versions of concepts and their variants

6. Contributions
- (1) framework for evaluating designs (regulators, designers, critics): dark when user's expected concept doesn't match application concept; prior approaches use deviation from expectations but don't say how expectations are obtained; concepts play this role
- (2) language for consensus standards: industry standards for best practices, e.g. PCI payment security, Web accessibility; concept catalogs give structure and language for conventional behaviors/interfaces of common units like shopping carts
- (3) design method: collaborative creation of catalogs + instantiation of concepts in a particular design; Alexander's programme in architecture; realized in software (code level) by community from the design patterns book

7. Roadmap and evaluation
- Section 2: taxonomies and theories of dark patterns, differences and synergies
- Section 3.1 software concepts; Sections 3.2, 3.3 darkness criteria; Section 4 concept catalogs
- three studies: Brignull's catalog, latest version (5.1); three shopping cart variants (5.2); sample concept vs. variants in popular web applications (5.3)
- Section 6.1 merits, 6.2 challenges, Section 7 next steps

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
When users run into deceptive design elements in applications, they can feel annoyed or frustrated, but they also feel resigned. There is a feeling that deception is so rampant that users just have to live with it. To counter this, practitioners came up with the term "dark pattern" to label the common tactics and idioms that are used to deceive users. They catalogued them and pointed to examples, hoping that exposing them would lead responsible designers to avoid them.

Researchers have recognized that this problem is important. They have investigated how often dark patterns occur, explored how users react to them and how designers decide to incorporate them or not, and more broadly they have developed theories that try to articulate what exactly makes a design "dark". But while doing this, a gap has opened between this rich body of research and the working practices of designers.

Partly this is because of a cultural divide, where ethical discussions are more common in academic settings, and partly it is because ethical guidelines are not easy to translate into practice, especially when they need subtle judgments about borderline cases.

Another reason, which is less recognized but maybe equally important, is that practitioners spend less time making fresh design decisions than academics often think. A lot of their effort is adopting (and adapting) large pieces of functionality and interaction design. In this respect the pattern-driven approach, which says "don't do things like this", may be more practical than theory-driven approaches that give more general criteria.

So pattern catalogs and theories have complementary benefits. Catalogs can be acted on readily: their contents are easy to evaluate, and usually they can be matched to the given circumstances and applied straightforwardly. Theories are less immediately applicable, but they give the underlying principles and the ethical justification for consensus viewpoints, and also a language for exploring edge cases when consensus is harder to reach.

But the existing catalogs of dark patterns have limitations. First, and most obviously, they tell a designer what not to do, when a designer usually wants advice on what to do. This makes a catalog less useful, and it also means that the larger community of designers misses an opportunity to publicize and inculcate good practices.

Second, the match between a pattern and an exact instantiation may be clear, but it can be harder to evaluate variant designs that share only some of the features of the pattern, or that present them in subtly different ways. For example, it is not clear if adding "suggested items" to a user's shopping cart violates the Sneak into Basket dark pattern.

Third, a catalog of negative patterns is necessarily incomplete. Making sure that a particular set of dark patterns is absent from a design cannot be enough to establish that the design is acceptable. This is the challenge of regulating against dark patterns. A well-intentioned company that has avoided the known dark patterns in its products should surely be able to have some confidence that it will not be sued for including design elements that might come to be regarded as dark but were never explicitly specified. The broad nature of some regulatory efforts makes this problem worse (for example, a recent EU white paper suggests that all forms of emotional steering are culpable).

In this paper we outline a new approach that combines aspects of patterns and of theory. The key idea is that acceptable designs are defined as instantiations of positive patterns, and deviations from them are treated as "dark." Our patterns are based on software concepts, which were introduced as a way to modularize application functionality.

A concept is a unit of functionality that offers a coherent and separable service to the user and fulfills a clear purpose. The concepts of an online store might include ShoppingCart, Order, Catalog, etc., and also less domain-specific concepts like UserAuthentication, Notification, Recommendation, etc. We propose to create concept catalogs that document the standard versions of concepts and their variants.

The contributions of this work are:

- (1) A framework for evaluating designs. Regulators, designers (and critics in general) can use our approach to evaluate designs. Roughly, a design is dark when the concept the user expects does not match the concept underlying the application. Many earlier approaches also define darkness as deviation from user expectations, but they do not say how those expectations are obtained. We show how concepts can play this role.

- (2) A language for consensus standards. Many industry groups have benefited from defining standards that capture best practices, for example the PCI standard for payment security and Web accessibility standards. Concept catalogs can give a structure and a language for articulating conventional behaviors and interfaces for common functional units like shopping carts.

- (3) A design method. For designers and developers, our approach suggests splitting design work into two aspects: creating catalogs collaboratively to describe existing concepts, and instantiating concepts from a catalog in the context of a particular design. This is the programme Alexander proposed for architecture, and it was realized in software (although at the code level) in the community that grew out of the design patterns book.

The paper starts by reviewing existing taxonomies and theories of dark patterns, and points to differences and synergies between them and our approach (Section 2). We explain our approach, starting with the idea of software concepts (Section 3.1), then defining criteria for darkness based on deviation from conventional concepts (Sections 3.2, 3.3), and then presenting the idea of catalogs of concepts (Section 4).

We evaluated our approach with three studies. First, we checked that it can account for uncontroversial negative examples by applying it to the latest version of Brignull's catalog (Section 5.1). Second, we analyze three shopping cart variants to test whether it can make nuanced distinctions (Section 5.2). Third, to check that a catalog concept can accommodate the real variety of instances, we build a sample concept and make sure it accommodates all the variants found in a repertoire of popular web applications (Section 5.3).

Finally, we discuss the merits of our approach (Section 6.1) and some challenges to it (Section 6.2), and we conclude with some ideas for next steps (Section 7).

steps.text:
When users experience deceptive design elements in applications, they may feel annoyed or frustrated—but they also feel resigned. There is a sense that deception is so rampant that users just have to live with it [1]. To counter this, practitioners coined the term "dark pattern" [2] to label the common tactics and idioms employed to deceive users, cataloging them and pointing to examples, in the hope that exposing them would lead responsible designers to shun them.

Recognizing the importance of this problem, researchers have investigated the incidence of dark patterns [3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10]; explored how users react to them [11,12,1,13,14,15] and how designers choose to incorporate them (or not) [16,17]; and more broadly have developed theories that seek to articulate exactly what makes a design "dark" [18,19]. In so doing, a gap has opened between this rich body of research and the working practices of designers [20].

This is partly due to a cultural divide, with ethical discussions more prevalent in academic settings, and partly because ethical guidelines are not easily translated into practice, especially when they require subtle judgments about borderline cases.

Less recognized, but perhaps equally important, is that practitioners spend less time making fresh design decisions than academics often assume. Much of their effort involves adopting (and adapting) large pieces of functionality and interaction design. In this respect, the pattern-driven approach that says "don't do things like this" may be more practical than theory-driven approaches that offer more general criteria.

Pattern catalogs and theories thus have complementary benefits. Catalogs are readily actionable: their contents are easily evaluated, and they can usually be matched to given circumstances and applied straightforwardly. Theories, though less immediately applicable, provide the underlying principles and ethical justification for consensus viewpoints, and a language for exploring edge cases when consensus is harder to come by.

The existing catalogs of dark patterns, however, have limitations. First, and most obviously, they tell a designer what not to do, when a designer is usually seeking advice on what to do. This not only makes a catalog less useful but also means the larger community of designers is missing an opportunity to publicize and inculcate good practices.

Second, although the match between a pattern and an exact instantiation may be clear, it can be harder to evaluate variant designs that share only some of the pattern's features, or that present them in subtly different ways. It is unclear, for example, whether adding "suggested items" to a user's shopping cart violates the Sneak into Basket dark pattern [21].

Third, a catalog of negative patterns is necessarily incomplete. Ensuring that a particular set of dark patterns is absent from a design cannot be sufficient to establish that the design is acceptable. Herein lies the challenge of regulating against dark patterns. A well-intentioned company that has avoided known dark patterns in its products is surely entitled to some confidence that it will not be sued for including design elements that might come to be regarded as dark but were never explicitly specified. This problem is made worse by the broad nature of some regulatory efforts (for example, the suggestion in a recent EU white paper [22] that all forms of emotional steering are culpable).

In this paper, we outline a new approach that combines aspects of both patterns and theory. The key idea is to define acceptable designs as instantiations of positive patterns, with deviations from them treated as "dark." Our patterns are based on software concepts [23], which were introduced as a way to modularize application functionality.

A concept is a unit of functionality that offers a coherent and separable service to the user, fulfilling a clear purpose. An online store's concepts might include ShoppingCart, Order, Catalog, etc., as well as less domain-specific concepts such as UserAuthentication, Notification, Recommendation, etc. We propose creating concept catalogs that document standard versions of concepts and their variants.

The contributions of this work are:

- (1) A framework for evaluating designs. Regulators, designers (and critics more generally) can use our approach to evaluate designs. Roughly, a design is dark when the user's expected concept does not match the underlying application concept. Many prior approaches likewise define darkness as deviation from user expectations, but do not indicate how those expectations are obtained. We show how concepts can play this role.

- (2) A language for consensus standards. Many industry groups have benefited from defining standards that capture best practices; notable examples include the PCI standard for payment security [24] and Web accessibility standards [25]. Concept catalogs can provide a structure and language for articulating conventional behaviors and interfaces for common functional units such as shopping carts.

- (3) A design method. As a method for designers and developers, our approach suggests separating design work into two aspects: the collaborative creation of catalogs describing existing concepts, and the instantiation of concepts from a catalog in the context of a particular design. This is the programme Alexander proposed in the context of architecture [26], and that was realized in software (albeit at the code level) in the community that grew out of the design patterns book [27].

Our paper begins by reviewing existing taxonomies and theories of dark patterns, pointing to differences and synergies between them and our approach (Section 2). We explain our approach, starting with the idea of software concepts (Section 3.1), defining criteria for darkness based on deviation from conventional concepts (Sections 3.2, 3.3), and then presenting the idea of catalogs of concepts (Section 4).

We evaluated our approach in three studies. First, we checked that it can account for uncontroversial negative examples by applying it to the latest version of Brignull's catalog (Section 5.1). Second, we analyze three shopping cart variants to test its ability to make nuanced distinctions (Section 5.2). Third, to check that a catalog concept can accommodate the real variety of instances, we construct a sample concept and make sure it accommodates all the variants found in a repertoire of popular web applications (Section 5.3).

Finally, we discuss the merits of our approach (Section 6.1) and some challenges to it (Section 6.2), and conclude with some ideas about next steps (Section 7).
